docs.title: Porthole
docs.text:
Porthole lets you follow and control Claude Code and Codex sessions from a phone. A daemon runs on the machine where the agents run. The app connects to it over your LAN or VPN on TCP port 7433, reads the agents' own transcript files, and sends input into the session's tmux window. From the phone you can read a conversation including tool calls and thinking, type prompts and slash commands, open a terminal view of the tmux pane, answer Claude Code permission prompts and plan approvals, change the permission mode, run a command Claude suggested and see its output, send a photo for Claude to look at, watch the subagents a session has started, start a new session in a repository, and, with claude-swap installed, see which account is active and how much quota is left.

The daemon listens only on loopback, private and VPN addresses. Phones pair with a single-use QR code and pin the daemon's certificate. The details are on the security page.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text: Piece Where it runs What it does Daemon (porthole) the computer that runs Claude Code or Codex: Linux, macOS, or Windows through WSL2 watches transcript files, drives tmux, brokers permission prompts, serves the app over TLS on port 7433 App Android or iOS lists sessions, renders conversations, sends input, answers permission prompts Network between the two any private network the phone can reach the computer on: the same Wi-Fi, WireGuard, Tailscale, NetBird Push relay (optional) a Cloudflare Worker, hosted by the project or by you wakes the phone while the app is closed; receives only ciphertext

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
On the computer:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
cd ~/code/my-project && porthole add     # optional; pairing works without it
porthole pair                            # prints a QR code

On the phone, install the app (see The app for the beta links), tap Scan pairing code and point it at the QR. The longer version:

  1. Install the daemon
  2. Pair a phone
  3. The app

Store and beta links for the app are on The app. Source code and daemon releases: https://github.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole.

docs.title: The app
docs.text: The Porthole app runs on Android and iOS. It talks to the daemons you paired with and, if you turn it on, to a push relay. It has no accounts and no purchases.

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
• iOS: join the beta through the public TestFlight link, https://testflight.apple.com/join/wYZrvvYa. The link becomes active after Apple's beta review. If TestFlight says the beta is not accepting testers yet, try again later.
  • Android: the Play closed test link will be added here once the test track is live. Until then, build the app yourself.

docs.title: Build it yourself
docs.text: app/ is a Flutter project. flutter build apk or flutter build ipa gives you a build without push. To build with push against your own Firebase project and relay, follow Build the app yourself.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
The empty home screen offers two things:

  • Scan pairing code starts pairing.
  • Try the demo loads a sample machine with canned sessions so you can look around before pairing.

docs.title: Home
docs.text: Home lists every session from every connected machine, filtered by All, a machine, Claude or Codex. Each row shows a glyph and a word for what the session is doing: blue means working, amber means it is waiting for you, green means ready and grey means it has ended. The (i) button explains every glyph; so does Reading the states. Sessions that need you (a permission prompt, a question, a plan to approve) move to the top with a badge. Finished sessions are under History. New session starts an agent on a repository of a connected machine. A machine's menu offers Connect now, Accounts & usage, Open machine view and Manage machines.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
The session screen renders the conversation from the CLI's own transcript: prompts, replies, tool calls and results, and with Show thinking the model's thinking. It opens at the bottom unless you change Open chats at in Settings, and while you are at the bottom it stays there as new messages and images arrive. Scroll up to Load earlier. The input bar types into the session's tmux window, so slash commands and your own skills work as they do at the keyboard.

  • Terminal view switches to the live tmux pane for menus, prompts and anything the chat view cannot show, with a key bar for Enter, Escape, arrows and control keys.
  • Interrupt (Esc) stops the agent mid-turn.
  • Resume in tmux… restarts a finished session inside tmux so it becomes controllable.
  • A permission request appears as a card with the tool name and input and Allow and Deny buttons. A prompt the terminal is already showing, or a plan waiting for approval, appears as a card with the same choices the terminal offers; see permission prompts.
  • The mode chip in the header (Manual, Edits, Plan, Auto) shows the session's permission mode. Tap it to change it; see Permission mode.
  • A shell command in one of Claude's replies has Copy, Run with ! and Run in a window under it. Either run path shows you the command and asks before running; see Running a suggested command. Commands run with !, from the phone or at the keyboard, appear in the chat as a command block with their output.
  • A message you send while Claude is busy shows at once as a faded bubble marked "Queued", and so do messages queued at the keyboard; see Messages sent while Claude is busy.
  • The attach button in the message box sends a photo or a picture from the library for Claude to look at. Images in the conversation show inline; tap one to see it full size. See Images.
  • A session that has started subagents shows a strip under its title with their count, how many are still working and their tokens. Tap it for the list; see Subagents.

The header shows the machine, session status, repository, model and the account doing the work. A session that is not running inside tmux shows a read-only notice; see Sessions.

docs.title: New session
docs.text: Pick the machine, Claude Code or Codex, a repository (see choosing where sessions start), a permission mode for Claude Code (Default (ask), Plan mode, Accept edits) and an optional first prompt. The session runs inside a tmux session you can also attach to from a terminal.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Machines shows one entry per paired daemon with its reported name, version and running sessions. Rename it, toggle Auto-connect (connect when the app opens), Mute notifications (no alerts or push from this machine), Connect now, or Forget it. Pair machine adds another.

Each entry lists the machine's addresses as the daemon advertises them, with the result of the last check and which one carries the connection. Tap an address to prefer it. Hold one for Ignore this address: the app stops dialling and checking it, and it stays in the list struck through until you hold it again and choose Stop ignoring. Addresses the daemon stops advertising drop out of the list on the next connection by themselves. This is the only place the app talks about addresses; everywhere else a machine is just online, reconnecting, offline or unreachable.

docs.title: Accounts & usage
docs.text: With claude-swap installed on the machine, this page shows which account is active, how much of each quota window is used and when it resets. Codex rate limits appear when the CLI reports them. Pull down to refresh; the back arrow returns to the list.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• Open chats at chooses where a conversation opens: Bottom (the newest message, the default), Top of the last message (the start of Claude's latest reply), or Last read position (where you left off, with a thin "New since you were here" line above anything that arrived since). The position is remembered on the phone for each session.
  • Notify while connected shows local notifications for permission prompts and input requests while the app is open or kept alive.
  • Stay connected in the background (Android) runs a foreground service that keeps the connection to the daemon open, with a persistent notification. Alerts then arrive from the daemon directly, without a relay.
  • Push relay enables notifications while the app is closed. See Push notifications.
  • Machines opens the same list as above.
  • Links to the privacy policy, terms of service and source code.

docs.title: Install the daemon
docs.text:
The daemon runs on the computer where Claude Code or Codex runs, as your own user. It needs:

  • Linux, macOS, or Windows through WSL2.
  • tmux, for sessions you want to control from the phone.
  • claude and/or codex on your PATH.
  • A private address the phone can reach: the same Wi-Fi, or a VPN such as WireGuard, Tailscale or NetBird. The daemon never listens on a public address.

docs.title: One-line installer
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

The script downloads the latest GitHub release for your OS and architecture, verifies the checksum, and runs porthole install.

To build from source instead, with Go 1.27:

cd daemon
go build -o ~/.local/bin/porthole ./cmd/porthole
porthole install

docs.title: What porthole install does
docs.text:
1. Copies the running binary to ~/.local/bin/porthole if it is not already there.
  2. Sets up a user service so the daemon starts at login and restarts if it crashes. Sessions started from the app run in tmux outside the service, so restarting or upgrading the daemon leaves them running:
    • Linux: writes ~/.config/systemd/user/porthole.service, runs systemctl --user daemon-reload and systemctl --user enable --now porthole, then tries loginctl enable-linger so the service also runs while you are logged out. If linger needs root it prints the sudo command to run.
    • macOS: writes ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon.plist and loads it.
  3. Runs the same checks as porthole doctor: tmux, the CLIs, the profiles it will watch, and whether the daemon answers.
  4. Installs the Claude Code hooks and the Codex notify handler, the same as porthole install-hooks. The hooks deliver permission prompts and session status to the daemon. They apply to sessions started after this point.
  5. Prints the next steps: porthole add inside a repository, then porthole pair.

porthole install --no-service skips step 2 (run porthole serve yourself, or use the unit files under daemon/packaging/). --no-hooks skips step 4.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Run the one-line installer again. It downloads the newest release, replaces ~/.local/bin/porthole, restarts the service and refreshes the hooks. Sessions keep running through the restart, with one exception: the service installed by version 0.1.0 stopped the sessions it had started when it was restarted, so the upgrade from 0.1.0 ends sessions you started from the app (not ones you started in a terminal). Finish or detach those first. Every later upgrade leaves them alone.

The app and the daemon move together. App version 1.0 needs daemon 0.2.0 or newer; porthole status prints the version you are running, and the changelog lists what each release added.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
porthole status

prints the version, the addresses the daemon is listening on, and how many sessions and devices it knows about. porthole doctor goes through the environment in more detail.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text: The app connects to TCP port 7433 (change it with port in config.toml). If the computer runs a host firewall, allow that port on the VPN or LAN interface the phone will use.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Tell the daemon about your repositories with porthole add. Directories you have already run an agent in are offered without it.
  • Pair a phone.

docs.title: Pair a phone
docs.text: Pairing gives the phone a device token and the daemon's certificate fingerprint. It happens once per phone and machine. After that the app reconnects on its own.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The daemon is running: porthole status answers.
  • The phone can reach the computer on a private address: the same Wi-Fi network, or a VPN such as WireGuard, Tailscale or NetBird. The daemon refuses connections from public addresses.
  • TCP port 7433 is open in the computer's firewall on that interface.

docs.title: Scan the code
docs.text:
On the computer:

porthole pair

prints a QR code, how long it is valid, and the same values as text:

Scan with the Porthole app within 2m0s.
Manual entry: host 100.64.0.5 or 192.168.1.20  port 7433  code ABCDEFGH
Certificate fingerprint: …

In the app, tap Scan pairing code on the empty home screen, or Machines → Pair machine, and point the camera at the QR. The code is single use and expires after two minutes. Run porthole pair again if you miss the window.

If the output ends with warning: no VPN or private address is bound; is your VPN up?, the daemon found nothing but loopback to listen on. Bring the VPN up and restart the daemon.

docs.title: Enter the values by hand
docs.text:
Tap Enter manually on the pairing screen. The fields are:

Field From porthole pair Host (VPN address) one of the host values; pick the one on the network the phone is on Port port (7433 unless you changed it) Certificate fingerprint the Certificate fingerprint line Pairing code code This device's name any name; porthole devices lists it

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• porthole pair --label "pixel" attaches a label to the pairing.
  • porthole pair --json prints the pairing payload as JSON instead of a QR.

docs.title: What pairing establishes
docs.text:
• The app pins the daemon's self-signed TLS certificate by fingerprint and refuses any other certificate.
  • The app receives a random device token, stored in the phone's keychain or keystore. The daemon stores a hash of it.
  • The two sides agree on a key for encrypting push notices, so a relay cannot read them.

See Security for the full model.

docs.title: Manage paired devices
docs.text:
porthole devices              # ID, name, paired date, last seen
porthole devices revoke <id>  # closes that phone's connections within a second

On the phone, Machines lists every daemon you have paired: rename it, mute its notifications, turn auto-connect on or off, or forget it. One phone can pair with any number of machines; their sessions appear in one list.

docs.title: Windows (WSL2)
docs.text: There is no native Windows build. Session discovery reads /proc and runs ps, control goes through the tmux binary, and the service installer knows systemd and launchd only. On Windows, run the daemon inside a WSL2 distribution and run Claude Code or Codex inside the same distribution: the daemon reads their transcripts from ~/.claude and ~/.codex of the Linux home, so agents started from PowerShell or cmd are not seen. Everything on Install the daemon applies inside WSL2; this page covers what differs.

docs.title: Set up WSL2
docs.text:
Enable systemd so porthole install can register the user service. Inside the distribution:

sudo tee /etc/wsl.conf <<'EOT'
[boot]
systemd=true
EOT

If /etc/wsl.conf already exists, add the two lines to it instead of replacing it.

Then from PowerShell:

wsl --shutdown

Open the distribution again and confirm with systemctl --user status. Without systemd the service step fails and porthole install prints You can still run porthole serve by hand; run porthole install --no-service instead and start porthole serve in a tmux window yourself.

Install tmux:

sudo apt install tmux

The daemon needs it for every session you want to control from the phone.

Run the installer:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZerkerEOD/porthole/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

uname -s reports Linux inside WSL2, so the script takes the Linux path: it downloads the linux release for your architecture, verifies the checksum, and runs porthole install. The install step tries loginctl enable-linger; if that needs root it prints the sudo command to run.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: The phone must reach the daemon on a private address. The daemon accepts connections from loopback, link-local, RFC 1918, CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10, the range Tailscale uses) and IPv6 ULA addresses, and binds VPN interfaces by name (see Security). Pick one of these two setups.

docs.title: Tailscale inside WSL
docs.text:
Install Tailscale inside the distribution, not on Windows:

curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
sudo tailscale up

The distribution gets its own tailscale0 interface with a 100.x address. The daemon binds it and lists it first in the pairing QR, and the phone connects over the tailnet from anywhere. No Windows firewall change is needed because the traffic arrives through the tunnel.

docs.title: Mirrored networking and a firewall rule
docs.text:
Mirrored networking (Windows 11 22H2 or later) gives the distribution the same LAN address as the Windows host. Create or edit %UserProfile%\.wslconfig:

[wsl2]
networkingMode=mirrored

Then from PowerShell:

wsl --shutdown

Allow TCP 7433 through Windows Defender Firewall, from an elevated PowerShell:

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Porthole" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 7433 -Action Allow

Use the port you set in config.toml if you changed it. If the phone still cannot connect, allow inbound traffic to WSL in the Hyper-V firewall:

Set-NetFirewallHyperVVMSetting -Name '{40E0AC32-46A5-438A-A0B2-2B479E8F2E90}' -DefaultInboundAction Allow

docs.title: NAT mode is not supported
docs.text: The default WSL2 networking mode puts the distribution behind NAT with a 172.x address that the phone cannot reach. Forwarding the port with netsh interface portproxy does not help: the daemon sees the proxy as the connection source, so it cannot tell your phone from any other client, and the address it prints for pairing is still the unreachable one. Use one of the two setups above.

docs.title: Pair
docs.text:
Inside the distribution:

porthole pair

prints the QR code and a Manual entry: host ... line with the addresses the daemon chose. Check that line before scanning: with Tailscale it should show a 100.x address, with mirrored networking the LAN address of the Windows host. If it shows only a 172.x address, or ends with warning: no VPN or private address is bound, the networking step is not complete. Then follow Pair a phone.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The daemon runs only while the WSL instance runs. wsl --shutdown, a Windows reboot, or WSL stopping the distribution stops it. Open a WSL terminal to start the instance again; with systemd and lingering enabled the user service starts with it, otherwise run porthole serve.
  • Agents started on the Windows side (PowerShell, cmd, Windows Terminal without WSL) are not discovered. The daemon only sees processes and transcripts inside its own distribution.
  • porthole wrap, hooks and session control need tmux and claude or codex installed inside the distribution, on the Linux PATH.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
porthole is one binary: the daemon (porthole serve) and the commands that talk to it over a local socket. Run them as the user who owns the sessions, never as root.

Global flags, accepted by every command:

Flag Meaning --config <file> configuration file (default ~/.config/porthole/config.toml) --log-level <level> debug, info, warn or error (default info) --version print the version

docs.title: install
docs.text:
porthole install [--no-service] [--no-hooks]

Puts the running binary in ~/.local/bin/porthole if it is not already there, sets up a user service that starts the daemon at login, runs the doctor checks and installs the hooks, then prints what to do next.

  • Linux: writes ~/.config/systemd/user/porthole.service, runs systemctl --user daemon-reload and systemctl --user enable --now porthole, and tries loginctl enable-linger so the daemon runs while you are logged out (prints the sudo command if that fails).
  • macOS: writes ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon.plist and loads it.
Flag Meaning --no-service do not create or start a service --no-hooks skip install-hooks

docs.title: doctor
docs.text:
porthole doctor

Prints the config file in use, the workspaces, where tmux, claude, codex and cswap were found, each Claude Code and Codex profile the daemon will watch and whether the hooks are installed in it, and whether the daemon is running and on which addresses, with the interface and kind (loopback, lan, vpn) of each. Checks for an active host firewall (ufw, firewalld, nftables, iptables, or the macOS application firewall) and prints the command that opens the daemon's port in it.

docs.title: install-hooks
docs.text:
porthole install-hooks [--profile <dir>] [--codex-home <dir>] [--no-claude] [--no-codex]

Adds the Porthole hooks to Claude Code's settings.json and sets Codex's notify handler. Running it again changes nothing. Hooks take effect for new sessions; running sessions keep their old hook set.

Flag Meaning --profile <dir> CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR to install into (default ~/.claude) --codex-home <dir> CODEX_HOME to install into (default ~/.codex) --no-claude skip Claude Code --no-codex skip Codex

docs.title: uninstall-hooks
docs.text:
porthole uninstall-hooks [--profile <dir>]

Removes the hooks from Claude Code's settings. Codex's notify = [...] line is removed by hand.

docs.title: config
docs.text:
porthole config

Prints the configuration directory, state directory, socket path and the effective configuration as JSON.

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
porthole serve [--allow-public-bind-i-understand]

Runs the daemon in the foreground; the service runs this command. It refuses to start as root and refuses to bind a public address.

Flag Meaning --allow-public-bind-i-understand bind and accept connections on public addresses; see Security

docs.title: status
docs.text:
porthole status

Prints the version, machine name, pid, uptime, session and device counts, whether tmux and cswap were detected, the bound addresses with the interface and kind (loopback, lan, vpn) of each, the last ten connection attempts from phones (time, source address, path, result and device), and the last ten commands run from a phone with Run in a window (id, session, state, exit code and start time).

docs.title: sessions
docs.text:
porthole sessions [--json]

Lists the sessions the daemon knows about: provider, status, the tmux session when controllable, repository, title, last update and id. --json prints the raw records.

docs.title: pair
docs.text:
porthole pair [--label <text>] [--json]

Asks the running daemon for a one-time pairing code and prints it as a QR (porthole://pair?d=…) plus the manual values: hosts, port, code and certificate fingerprint. The code is single use and expires after two minutes. See Pair a phone.

Flag Meaning --label <text> optional label for this pairing --json print the pairing payload as JSON instead of a QR

docs.title: devices
docs.text:
porthole devices
porthole devices revoke <id>

Lists paired phones (id, name, paired date, last seen). revoke deletes one and closes its connections within a second.

docs.title: add
docs.text:
porthole add [dir] [--workspace] [--yes|-y]

Records a repository so the app can start sessions in it. With no argument it uses the current directory. It finds the git top level, shows it, asks to confirm, and writes it to ~/.config/porthole/repos.toml. A running daemon is told to reload at once; otherwise the change applies at the next start.

Flag Meaning --workspace record the directory as a workspace (a parent folder scanned two levels deep for git repositories) instead of a single repository --yes, -y do not ask for confirmation

docs.title: remove
docs.text:
porthole remove [dir]

Removes a repository or workspace recorded by add (current directory when omitted). Entries written by hand in config.toml are edited there.

docs.title: repos
docs.text:
porthole repos

Lists what the app will offer: configured repositories, repositories found under workspaces, and recent directories.

docs.title: wrap
docs.text:
porthole wrap <claude|codex> [args...]

Starts the CLI inside a tmux session in the current directory, so the app can control it, and attaches your terminal. Extra arguments are passed to the CLI. Inside tmux already, it opens a new window instead of nesting.

docs.title: Internal commands
docs.text: The hooks call porthole hook and porthole codex-notify. Both are hidden and exit without an error when the daemon is down, so the CLIs keep working. porthole client is a hidden developer tool: a pinned-TLS WebSocket client for exercising the protocol from the command line.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The daemon reads ~/.config/porthole/config.toml, or the file given with --config. The file is optional. With no file the daemon listens on every private address on port 7433, watches the default Claude Code and Codex profiles, and offers the repositories it has seen sessions in. porthole config prints the effective values and the paths in use.

Two files sit next to each other:

File Who writes it Holds config.toml you everything below; the CLI does not edit it repos.toml porthole add and porthole remove repos and workspaces lists, merged with the ones in config.toml

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The full example ships as daemon/packaging/config.example.toml:

# ~/.config/porthole/config.toml
name = "desktop"            # shown in the app
listen = ["auto"]           # every loopback/private/VPN address; or explicit IPs
port = 7433
workspaces = ["~/Programming"]   # parent dirs scanned two levels deep for git repos
repos = []                  # single repos to offer; `porthole add` writes them to repos.toml instead
                            # (directories you have already run claude/codex in appear automatically)
profiles = []               # extra CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR / CODEX_HOME dirs to watch

[claude]
enabled = true
binary = "claude"

[codex]
enabled = true
binary = "codex"

[tmux]
binary = "tmux"
session_prefix = "ph"       # spawned sessions are named ph-<provider>-<id>

[hooks]
permission_timeout_s = 60   # how long a permission prompt waits for a phone that is watching
permission_timeout_detached_s = 300  # ... when no terminal is attached and the phone must answer

[cswap]
enabled = true              # auto-off when cswap is not on PATH
poll_interval_s = 150       # cache reads; cswap owns the real network cadence

[push]
relay_url = ""              # empty = push off. The relay the app uses, without its credential
                            # (e.g. https://relay.zerkersec.io or your own Worker).

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Key Default Meaning name the hostname The machine name the app shows. listen ["auto"] auto binds every loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10), IPv6 ULA and VPN-interface address (tailscale*, wg*, utun*, tun*, nebula*, zt*). Give explicit IP addresses to bind only those. A public address is refused unless serve runs with --allow-public-bind-i-understand; see Security. port 7433 TCP port for the app. Open it in the host firewall on the interface the phone uses. workspaces none Parent directories scanned two levels deep for git repositories, offered in New session. ~ and environment variables are expanded. porthole add --workspace records the same thing in repos.toml. repos none Individual repositories offered in New session without scanning. porthole add records them in repos.toml; this key is for listing them by hand. profiles none Extra CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME directories to watch for transcripts, on top of ~/.claude, ~/.codex and anything a running process is using.

docs.title: [claude] and [codex]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning enabled true Turn the integration off. binary claude / codex Name or path of the CLI used to start new sessions.

docs.title: [tmux]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning binary tmux Name or path of tmux. session_prefix ph Sessions started from the app are named <prefix>-<provider>-<id>.

docs.title: [hooks]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning permission_timeout_s 60 How long a Claude Code permission prompt waits for a phone that has the session open before the terminal prompt takes over. permission_timeout_detached_s 300 The wait when no phone is watching, the session was opened from a phone, and no terminal is attached to its tmux session, so a push notification can be answered. With a terminal attached the prompt goes straight to the terminal; the phone can still answer it from the screen.

docs.title: [cswap]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning enabled true Read account and quota information from claude-swap. Off when cswap is not on PATH. binary cswap Name or path of the cswap binary. poll_interval_s 150 How often the daemon re-reads cswap's cached account list. cswap itself decides when to contact the network.

docs.title: [push]
docs.text: Key Default Meaning relay_url empty Base URL of the push relay, without the credential that sits in the app's relay URL: https://relay.zerkersec.io for the hosted relay, or your own Worker's URL. Empty means push is off and the daemon refuses push registrations from the app. See Push notifications.

docs.title: Reloading
docs.text:
The daemon reloads repos.toml and the workspaces list when porthole add or porthole remove asks it to, or on SIGHUP:

systemctl --user kill -s HUP porthole      # Linux
kill -HUP "$(pgrep -u "$USER" -f 'porthole serve')"

Every other key (port, listen, profiles, the provider, hook, cswap and push sections) needs a restart:

systemctl --user restart porthole                                              # Linux
launchctl kickstart -k "gui/$(id -u)/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon"            # macOS

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
What Where Override Configuration ~/.config/porthole/ (config.toml, repos.toml) XDG_CONFIG_HOME, --config State: TLS key and certificate, paired devices (devices.json), transcript cursors ~/.local/state/porthole/ (mode 0700) XDG_STATE_HOME Control socket for the CLI and hooks $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/porthole/porthole.sock, or <state>/run/ where there is no runtime dir (macOS) XDG_RUNTIME_DIR Service unit ~/.config/systemd/user/porthole.service (Linux), ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon.plist (macOS)

Deleting the state directory makes the daemon generate a new certificate and forget every paired phone. You then pair again.

docs.title: Push notifications
docs.text:
While the app is open, or kept alive on Android with Stay connected in the background, it receives permission prompts, questions and finished turns from the daemon over the VPN. Once the app is closed, and on iOS as soon as it leaves the foreground (see iOS background behavior), only the platform push service can reach it. That needs a server holding the app's push credentials: the push relay. Without a relay, alerts arrive only while the app is open.

A push goes only to phones that are not connected to that machine at that moment; a connected app gets the same event over the socket instead.

docs.title: What the relay sees
docs.text: The daemon encrypts a notice (session title, machine name, the kind of attention needed) with a key agreed at pairing and posts the ciphertext to the relay. The relay checks a signed grant and forwards the ciphertext through FCM to the phone, which decrypts it and shows the notification. The relay stores a push token, a random device id and a timestamp. The app fetches the details from your machine when you open it. See Security for the relay's place in the model.

docs.title: Use the hosted relay
docs.text:
A hosted relay runs at relay.zerkersec.io. Supporters get a personal relay URL from https://zerkersec.io/supporter, of the form

https://PH-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX@relay.zerkersec.io

The part before the @ is your relay credential. The app sends it to the relay as a bearer token. The phone gets the URL with the credential; each daemon gets the base URL without it, as shown below.

  1. On the phone, open Settings → Push relay, paste the URL and tap Connect. The app asks for notification permission, fetches a grant from the relay, and hands that grant to every paired machine.

  2. On each machine, set the relay's base URL (without the credential) in ~/.config/porthole/config.toml and restart the daemon:

    [push]
relay_url = "https://relay.zerkersec.io"

    systemctl --user restart porthole                                    # Linux and WSL2
launchctl kickstart -k "gui/$(id -u)/io.zerkersec.porthole.daemon"  # macOS

    A daemon with an empty relay_url refuses push registrations. The app then shows the relay as connected, but that machine never pushes.

docs.title: Run your own
docs.text: The app accepts any relay URL of the form https://[credential@]host[/path]. See Self-hosting the push relay. A relay you run needs an app built against your own Firebase project; see Build the app yourself.

docs.title: Relay status in Settings
docs.text:
Shown as Meaning Relay: connected A grant is held and renews itself. Push is on. Relay: not active The relay refused the credential (HTTP 402: not active, lapsed, or unknown). Check it with whoever runs the relay. Relay: could not verify The relay could not be reached. The app keeps the last grant if it has one and retries.

Grants last at most 30 days and the app renews one within three days of its expiry. If the relay answers 401, 403 or 410 (invalid grant, blocked device, push token gone), the app drops the stored grant and requests a fresh one. Re-check forces a renewal now. Remove relay forgets the URL and tells every machine to stop pushing.

docs.title: What is pushed
docs.text: The daemon pushes the same notices the app shows live: a permission prompt, a question, or a finished turn, once per wait, and only for sessions you opened from the phone (see Status and attention).

docs.title: Per-machine control
docs.text: Machines → Mute notifications drops that machine's grant, so it neither pushes nor raises live alerts. Unmuting restores it. The Push notifications switch in Settings turns push off for every machine without forgetting the relay.

docs.title: Builds without push
docs.text: Push works only when the Firebase options are compiled into the app. Store builds have them. A build made without --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json has no Push relay field in Settings and shows a note saying so. Notifications still work while the app is open, and on Android with Stay connected in the background.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: A session is one Claude Code or Codex conversation. The daemon finds sessions by reading the transcript files the CLIs write (~/.claude/projects and ~/.codex/sessions, plus any profiles you configure). Every session the CLIs record appears in the app, whether or not Porthole started it.

docs.title: Controllable or read-only
docs.text:
The app can read any session the daemon can see. It can type into a session only when that session runs inside tmux, because tmux is how the daemon delivers keystrokes and captures the screen. There are two ways to get a controllable session:

  • Start it from the terminal with porthole wrap:

    cd ~/code/my-project
porthole wrap claude            # or: porthole wrap codex
porthole wrap claude --resume   # extra arguments go to the CLI

    wrap opens a tmux session in the current directory and runs the CLI in it, attaching your terminal. If you are already inside tmux, it opens a new window instead of nesting.

  • Start it from the app with New session. These run inside tmux, named ph-<provider>-<id>, and you can attach to them from a terminal too.

A session started any other way (plain claude in a terminal, an IDE integration) is shown read-only: you can follow it, but the input bar and the terminal view are disabled. Once it has finished, Resume in tmux… restarts it under tmux and makes it controllable.

docs.title: Choosing where sessions start
docs.text:
New session lists the repositories the daemon offers. porthole repos prints the same list, which comes from three sources:

  1. Recent directories: every directory the daemon has seen a Claude Code or Codex session in, from the profiles it watches. These need no configuration.

  2. Repositories recorded with porthole add, or listed under repos in config.toml. Use this for a repository you have not run an agent in yet:

    cd ~/code/new-project
porthole add            # finds the git top level, asks to confirm
porthole add ~/code/other-project --yes

  3. Workspaces: parent folders scanned two levels deep for git repositories, recorded with porthole add --workspace ~/code or listed under workspaces in config.toml.

porthole add writes to ~/.config/porthole/repos.toml, a file the CLI manages. It does not edit config.toml. A running daemon picks the change up at once; otherwise it applies at the next start. porthole remove [dir] takes an entry out again (entries you wrote in config.toml yourself are edited there). The daemon logs a warning at start when no repositories or workspaces are configured; recent directories still work.

A new session's directory must be inside a configured repository or workspace, or be one of the recent directories. The app cannot start an agent in any other path.

docs.title: Hooks: permission prompts and status
docs.text:
porthole install (or porthole install-hooks) registers Porthole as a Claude Code hook for SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied and PostModelSwitch, and as the Codex notify handler. This is how the daemon learns a session's status (idle, busy, waiting for permission, waiting for input, exited) without polling, and how a permission prompt reaches the phone.

When Claude Code asks for permission, the hook tells the daemon, which decides who should answer:

  1. A phone has the session open: the daemon holds the prompt for permission_timeout_s (60 s by default) and shows it on the phone with the tool name and input. Tap Allow or Deny; the answer goes back through the hook, bound to that request's id.
  2. No phone is watching, but you opened the session from a phone and no terminal is attached to its tmux session: the daemon holds the prompt for permission_timeout_detached_s (5 minutes) and sends a push, so you have time to open the app and answer.
  3. A terminal is attached and no phone is watching: the hook returns at once and Claude Code draws its own prompt in the terminal, so the person at the keyboard is not kept waiting.

In the last case, and whenever a held prompt times out, the daemon reads the prompt off the terminal screen and shows it in the app with the same choices the terminal offers: Yes, Yes, and always allow…, Yes, and switch to auto mode, No, or for a plan Yes, and use auto mode, Yes, manually approve edits, Tell Claude what to change. Tapping one presses the matching keys in the terminal. If the daemon is not running, nothing is held and the terminal prompt appears as usual.

The plan approval dialog is never held by the hook, because a hook decision can only say yes or no. The daemon lets the terminal draw it, reads it back within a second or two, and shows the whole plan from the plan file on the card with the dialog's three choices. After Tell Claude what to change, type the change in the message box.

Hooks take effect for sessions started after they were installed; running sessions keep their old hook set. porthole uninstall-hooks removes them (remove Codex's notify line by hand).

docs.title: Permission mode
docs.text:
Each Claude session runs in a permission mode: Manual (ask before each tool), Accept edits, Plan, Auto, and the launch-only Don't ask and Bypass. The mode shows as a chip in the session header and after the status in the session list. Tap the chip to change it: the daemon presses Shift+Tab in the terminal until the status bar names the mode you chose, the same thing you would do at the keyboard. Auto is offered only when the account has it; Bypass only when the session was started with it. The mode cannot be changed while a prompt or question is open, because Tab means something else inside a dialog.

In auto mode, actions the classifier blocks never open a prompt; the session header notes the last one ("Auto mode blocked Bash, 2m ago") and the terminal lists them under /permissions. After several blocks Claude Code pauses auto mode and prompts normally, which the app then shows as above.

docs.title: Where a chat opens
docs.text: A chat opens at the bottom, and stays pinned there while you are at the bottom, so new messages and images that finish loading never leave you a screen above the end. Open chats at in Settings can change that to the top of Claude's latest reply, or to where you left off: the app remembers, per session and only on the phone, which message was at the top of the screen when you last scrolled, and draws a thin "New since you were here" line above anything that arrived after that. If the remembered message is far back, the app loads a few earlier pages to find it, and falls back to the bottom with a short note if it cannot.

docs.title: Messages sent while Claude is busy
docs.text:
Claude Code does not interrupt a turn for a new message. Type one while it is working, at the keyboard or from the phone, and the CLI holds it in a queue, draws it above the spinner, and sends it when the turn ends or when it next reports back from a tool. A queued message is not in the transcript yet, so the app cannot read it from there. Instead it shows it two ways.

  • A message you send from the phone appears at the bottom of the chat as soon as you tap send, faded, with a line under it: "Sending…", then "Queued · sends when Claude finishes the current turn" while the session is busy. When the message reaches the transcript the placeholder is replaced by the real one. If the daemon could not type it, the bubble says why and offers Retry.
  • Messages queued from anywhere else, including the keyboard and another phone, are read off the terminal screen by the daemon and shown the same way, in the order they will be sent. They disappear when the CLI sends them.

While messages are queued, Run with ! is unavailable, because the ! command would only join the queue behind them; the block says how many are ahead. Run in a window still works. To send the queued messages at once, open the terminal view and tap Send now on the key bar; it presses ctrl+x ctrl+s, the CLI's own key for that.

docs.title: Running a suggested command
docs.text:
When Claude's reply contains a shell block, the block carries three actions: Copy, Run with ! and Run in a window. Both run paths show the exact command first and wait for you to confirm.

Run with ! uses a feature of Claude Code itself: a line that starts with ! is run in a shell instead of being sent to the model, and the command and its output are written into the conversation, so Claude sees them on its next turn. The app asks the daemon to type ! into the session, wait for the terminal to show its shell prompt, then type the command and press Enter, exactly what you would do at the keyboard. The chat shows the result as a command block: the command line, then its output, then any errors. Because ! only works while the session is waiting at its prompt, the action is greyed out while Claude is working, and if the terminal does not switch to its shell prompt within a second or two the daemon takes the ! back and tells you the session is busy or has unsent text in its input box. The action is offered only for blocks whose lines are plain commands (no heredocs, no line continuations); several lines are joined with &&.

Run in a window is for long commands, multi-line blocks, or a session that is busy. The daemon opens a new window in the session's tmux session, runs the command there and streams the last lines into a card under the session header, with Stop, Open window and Dismiss. Open window shows that window in the terminal view while the command runs; Back to session returns to the session's own pane. When the command exits, the daemon types one message into the session with the command, the last 120 lines of output and the exit code, so the result reaches Claude the same way a pasted message would. If the session was busy, Claude Code queues that message as the next turn and the card says so. Switch Send output to the session off in the confirmation to keep the output on the card only. The finished window stays in tmux, named ph-run- and the run's id, for ten minutes and is then closed; Dismiss closes it at once. The daemon only ever closes windows it opened itself. The card keeps the output either way.

Both actions run with your account on the machine, exactly as typing into the terminal would; the daemon logs every run with the device that asked and the exit code, and porthole status lists the last ten.

Runs are written to disk, so a command that restarts the daemon itself (a rebuild followed by porthole install) is picked up by the new daemon: it finishes the card, sends the output to the session if you asked for it, and closes the window after ten minutes. A card marked "recovered" went through that. Full output on a finished card shows the whole log.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Images travel both ways between the phone and the machine, and never anywhere else.

  • The attach button in the message box takes a photo or picks one from the library, uploads it to the daemon, and adds an "Attached image:" line with the file's path to your message. Claude reads the file from there with its Read tool, so you can ask about a screenshot, a whiteboard or an error on another screen. PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF up to 10 MB are accepted. Uploads live under the daemon's state directory in uploads/<session id>/, readable only by your user, and are removed after seven days.
  • Images in the transcript are shown inline: what you pasted in the terminal and what Claude looked at with its Read tool. Tap one to view it full size. Images over 1.5 MB are listed by size instead of shown.
  • An image Claude writes and refers to by path, or embeds in markdown, is fetched from the machine and shown inline. The daemon serves only image files under the session's directory, its uploads folder, or its scratch space, and only to a paired phone.

docs.title: Subagents
docs.text:
When Claude Code hands work to a subagent (its Agent tool), the CLI writes that agent's transcript to its own file next to the session's. The daemon reads those files, so a session with subagents shows a strip under its title: "3 agents · 2 working · 190k tokens". Tap it for the list: each agent's type, what it was asked to do, how long it has run, tokens in and out, tool uses and its last line of output. Open one to read its transcript as it is written.

Subagents run inside the session's own process and have no input of their own, so the agent view is read-only. To steer one, message the session; Message the session on the agent view puts an opening line in the composer for you. When a background agent finishes, the session's chat shows one line with its summary, tokens, tool uses and duration.

The session's own token total (without its agents) appears at the end of the header line once the daemon has read it.

docs.title: Reading the states
docs.text:
A session row shows a glyph and a word for what the agent is doing. The colours mean one thing each: blue is working, amber is waiting for you, green is ready, grey is over, and crimson is reserved for errors.

Glyph Label Meaning spinning ring working The CLI is busy. With subagents the label counts them. filled question mark needs your answer A multiple-choice question is open. shield needs approval A permission prompt is waiting. checklist plan ready to approve Plan mode has written a plan and asks how to proceed. speech bubble waiting for you The turn ended; the session waits for your next message. check ready Idle, nothing pending. stop ended The CLI exited. Resume in tmux… restarts it. eye (trailing) read-only Not inside tmux, so the app can watch but not type. crimson corner mark blocked … Auto mode refused an action in the last 15 minutes.

Machines use a different set: a link for online, a spinning sync for connecting or reconnecting, a broken link for offline (crimson when every address failed its last check), and a warning sign for "pair again". The same table is in the app under the (i) button on the home screen.

docs.title: Status and attention
docs.text:
Each session carries a status: idle, busy, waiting_permission, waiting_input, exited or unknown. Sessions that need you sort to the top of the home screen.

Notifications follow three rules. They are sent only for sessions you opened from the phone: started with New session, or viewed in the app at least once. They are sent only when the session needs you: a permission prompt, a question, or a turn that has finished and is waiting for your next message. Each of those sends one notice per wait; a new message from you starts the next wait. A turn that ends while subagents or background commands are still running is not finished: the notice waits until that work is done and the session has stayed idle for a moment, and if the work wakes Claude again nothing is sent. Sessions running in your own terminals that you never opened in the app stay silent.

With Notify while connected on, the app raises those notices itself while it is open, and on Android also in the background when Stay connected in the background is on. For notifications while the app is closed, see Push notifications.

docs.title: Multiple machines
docs.text: Pair the phone with each machine. Each runs its own daemon with its own pairing. The app merges their sessions into one list and lets you filter by machine.

docs.title: Accounts and usage
docs.text: If claude-swap is on the machine's PATH, the daemon reads its cached account list. The app shows the active account and quota windows under Accounts & usage and tags each session with the account doing the work. Turn this off with [cswap] enabled = false in config.toml.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Releases of the daemon are on GitHub. The app ships through the App Store and Google Play; its version is shown in Settings, About.

Needs app 1.0 or newer. If you upgrade from 0.1.0, read the upgrading note first.

What you can do from the phone that you could not before:

  • Answer Claude Code's questions. When Claude asks you to choose between options, the choices appear in the chat and your answer is typed into the session. Questions that are only visible in the terminal are read from the screen and offered the same way.
  • Approve plans, with the full plan shown on the card, and change the permission mode (manual, accept edits, plan, auto) from the session header.
  • Run a command Claude suggested, either inside the session with Claude's own ! shortcut or in a separate window whose output is sent back into the conversation.
  • Send a photo for Claude to look at, and see images Claude refers to inline.
  • See the subagents a session has started, and a short summary when one finishes.
  • See the messages you sent while Claude was busy, queued in order, before the session picks them up. The terminal view has a "Send now" key for them.
  • Choose where a chat opens: at the bottom, at the start of Claude's latest reply, or where you left off, with a marker above what is new since then.

Smaller changes:

  • Session rows and machine chips use one set of states and icons; a legend explains them. Busy is blue, attention is amber.
  • The app tries the LAN and VPN addresses of a machine at the same time and shows which one answered. porthole status lists the addresses the daemon is listening on and the last connection attempts; porthole doctor mentions the firewall port.
  • Push notifications go only to phones that opened the session, once per thing that needs you.
  • Restarting or upgrading the daemon no longer stops the sessions it started.
  • porthole add, porthole remove and porthole repos manage the repositories offered when you start a session; porthole install waits for the daemon to come up before running its checks.

First release: the daemon with pairing, the session list, the conversation and terminal views, permission prompts on the phone, new sessions from the app, several machines in one list, the optional push relay, and account usage through claude-swap.

docs.title: iOS background behavior
docs.text:
iOS suspends an app's network connections shortly after it leaves the foreground. Porthole keeps its WebSocket to the daemon open while the app is visible and for the grace period iOS allows afterwards. After that nothing can arrive from the daemon directly.

  • With the app open, permission prompts and "needs input" states appear live.
  • With the phone locked or the app in the background, nothing arrives until you open the app again. The app then reconnects and shows the current state.
  • Android can keep the connection alive with a foreground service; see Stay connected in the background.

The only way to wake an iOS app from outside is Apple's push service, which requires a server holding the app's push key. That is the role of the push relay: the daemon sends an encrypted notice through the relay, the phone receives it as a notification, and the app fetches the details from your machine when you open it. See Push notifications.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page describes how Porthole secures the paths between the phone, the daemon, the agent CLIs and the optional push relay. The pairing steps are in Pair a phone and the push setup is in Push notifications.

docs.title: Components and boundaries
docs.text:
The phone app talks to the daemon over a WebSocket on a LAN or VPN address, with TLS 1.3 and a self-signed certificate the app pins at pairing. The daemon runs as the user who owns the agent sessions and refuses to start as root. It reads agent transcripts from disk, receives hook events over a local unix socket, drives terminals through tmux, and, when a relay URL is configured, posts encrypted notices to the relay, which forwards them through FCM. The phone and the hook process cross a boundary (the pinned certificate with the device token, and the socket file permission); the daemon and the user's tmux panes and transcript files do not, since the daemon has the same access as the user.

[Phone app] ──wss, TLS 1.3, pinned certificate, bearer device token──┐
   (LAN or VPN address only)                                          ▼
                                                      [porthole daemon, runs as the user]
                                                        │        │           │
   transcript JSONL (read only) ◄───────────────────────┘        │           └──► [tmux] send-keys, paste-buffer, capture-pane
   <profile>/projects, <codex home>/sessions                     │
                                                                 │
   [agent CLI hook process] ──unix socket, mode 0600────────────►┘
                                                                 │
   [relay (Cloudflare Worker)] ◄──https {grant, ciphertext, collapse}──┘  (only when push.relay_url is set)
          │
          └──► [FCM] ──► [Apple or Google push service] ──► [Phone]

docs.title: Phone authentication
docs.text:
porthole pair asks the daemon over the local socket for a pairing code and prints a QR code carrying the daemon name, the advertised addresses, the port, the certificate fingerprint and the code. The code is 8 characters of base32 from 5 random bytes, valid for 120 seconds, and deleted on first use. The daemon keeps only a SHA-256 hash of it in memory and compares hashes in constant time. A source address that fails five times in one minute is refused until the window passes, and POST /v1/pair as a whole admits one request every two seconds with a burst of ten.

A successful pairing returns a device id and a 32-byte random token, base64url encoded, sent to the app once. The daemon stores the token's SHA-256 in devices.json (mode 0600, written through a temporary file and a rename) under the state directory, $XDG_STATE_HOME/porthole or ~/.local/state/porthole, mode 0700. The app stores the token with the hosts, port and fingerprint in the platform keystore. Every request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>; a WebSocket client may instead pass it as the subprotocol porthole.token.<token>. Tokens do not expire. porthole devices lists paired devices and porthole devices revoke <id> removes one; the daemon closes that device's open connections within one second, and the app treats the next 401 as a revocation and asks the user to pair again.

On first run the daemon generates an ECDSA P-256 self-signed certificate valid for ten years and writes tls.crt and tls.key to the state directory with mode 0600. The fingerprint in the QR code is the base64url SHA-256 of the certificate's DER encoding. The app builds its TLS context with no trusted roots and accepts a certificate only when its fingerprint matches the stored one; a different certificate fails the handshake and the app reports "Certificate changed. Pair again." The daemon accepts TLS 1.3 only. Deleting tls.crt and tls.key and restarting the daemon rotates the certificate, and every phone must then re-pair.

docs.title: Network exposure
docs.text:
With the default listen = ["auto"] the daemon binds every loopback, link-local IPv4, RFC 1918, CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10) and IPv6 ULA address on an interface that is up, plus every address on an interface whose name starts with tailscale, wg, utun, tun, nebula or zt; interfaces named docker, br-, veth, virbr, lxc, cni, flannel or podman are skipped. 127.0.0.1 is always bound, the list is re-evaluated every ten seconds so a VPN interface that appears later is picked up, and the default port is 7433. An explicit listen address outside those ranges is refused at startup unless porthole serve is given --allow-public-bind-i-understand. Independently of binding, every accepted request is checked against the same address classes and a public source address receives 403 unless that flag is set. Without a valid token a caller reaches only POST /v1/pair; every other route returns 401 with an empty body.

The control socket porthole.sock lives in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/porthole (or run/ under the state directory when that variable is unset), with the directory at 0700 and the socket at 0600. It carries the CLI commands (pair, devices, revoke, status, config reload) and the hook events, with no authentication beyond the file permission: any process running as the same user can use it, which equals that user's shell access.

docs.title: What a phone can do
docs.text:
Every paired phone holds the same rights; there are no per-device scopes. Over the WebSocket a phone can:

  • list sessions, including title and working directory, and subscribe to the transcript events and the tmux screen of any session the daemon discovers;
  • page through transcript history (the daemon only reads transcript files);
  • send text to a session that has a tmux pane. The daemon passes the text to send-keys -l (or set-buffer and paste-buffer for multi-line text) as a separate argument, never through a shell, and takes the pane id from its own session list rather than from the client;
  • press named keys from a fixed allowlist (Enter, Escape, arrows, C-c and the like) or single printable characters, up to 32 per message;
  • answer a pending permission prompt with allow or deny. The daemon holds the hook open only while a phone subscribes to that session, gives each prompt a random id, and accepts an answer only for an id that is still pending. After hooks.permission_timeout_s (default 60) the hook returns no decision and the terminal prompt appears as usual;
  • start a session. The daemon builds the argv itself from the configured binary, the --resume, --permission-mode and --model values (at most 64 characters each, letters, digits and -_.:[] only), and the prompt after --. The directory passes insideWorkspace in daemon/internal/core/registry.go: after symlink resolution it is inside a configured workspace or an added repository, or it is exactly a directory an agent session has already run in;
  • register or clear its push grant.

Per connection the daemon reads at most 64 KiB per message, allows 60 messages per second with a burst of 120, admits four connections per device, and coalesces screen snapshots per session so a fast terminal cannot queue unbounded output.

A stolen phone or token therefore reads code and conversations, types into running agents, answers their permission prompts and starts new agents in the allowed directories, from any address that reaches the daemon. There is no second factor; the mitigation is porthole devices revoke, which takes effect within a second, and keeping the daemon reachable only over the VPN.

Hook events arrive through porthole hook, which porthole install-hooks registers for the session, prompt, stop, notification and permission events, and through the Codex notify program porthole codex-notify, which only reports completed turns. The daemon acts on a hook only when its transcript_path, after symlink resolution, lies under the projects directory of a watched profile; otherwise it logs a warning and returns no decision.

docs.title: Push relay
docs.text:
Push is off until push.relay_url names an https URL. At pairing the app generates an X25519 key pair and sends the public key; the daemon generates its own pair, derives a 32-byte key with HKDF-SHA256 over the shared secret and the info string porthole-push-v1, stores that key in devices.json, returns its public key and discards its private key. The app derives the same key and stores it in the keystore.

A notice is a JSON object with the kind (permission, input or done), the session key, the title clipped to 80 characters, the daemon name and a timestamp. The daemon seals it with XChaCha20-Poly1305 under the pairing key with a random 24-byte nonce; the ciphertext is capped at 480 bytes. The relay, FCM and the platforms carry only that ciphertext, and the APNs alert text is the fixed "A session needs your attention".

The app obtains a grant with POST /v1/grant, sending a random device id it generates, the platform, the FCM registration token, and the credential from the relay URL's userinfo as a bearer token. The relay limits grant requests to 5 per minute per client IP, rejects device ids on its deny list, optionally requires platform attestation (ATTEST_MODE; android verifies Play Integrity, iOS verification is not implemented, so all refuses iOS), and asks the entitlement service (an HTTPS endpoint sharing ENTITLEMENT_SECRET) or, on a self-hosted relay, a static list of credential SHA-256 hashes whether the credential is active. The grant is the JSON payload {v, d, t, p, iat, exp} base64url encoded, a dot, and an Ed25519 signature over that encoding made with a key held as a Worker secret; GET /v1/pubkey returns the verification key. It expires at the end of the entitlement period or after 30 days, whichever is sooner. The app registers the grant with each daemon over the WebSocket and renews it when fewer than three days remain.

The daemon posts {grant, ct, collapse} to POST /v1/push for each device that holds a live grant and is not connected, at most once per device, session and kind every 45 seconds; collapse is the first 32 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the session key. The relay verifies the signature and expiry, checks the deny list, enforces 10 pushes per minute per device id and 300 per day (a KV counter that expires after two days), and forwards to FCM. A 400 or 404 from FCM becomes a 410, on which the daemon drops the grant.

At grant time the relay sees the relay credential, device id, platform, push token and client IP; per push it sees the grant contents, the ciphertext, the collapse digest and the time. It keeps no subscriber list; its KV namespace holds the deny list (device ids the operator writes) and the daily counters. Rotating the signing key invalidates every grant at once. A self-hosted relay runs the same code with the static credential list in place of the entitlement service; the encryption, grant format and limits are unchanged.

docs.title: Threat summary
docs.text: Threat Control Residual risk Public internet exposure Bind and source-address policy admit only loopback, private, CGNAT, ULA and VPN addresses; public addresses need --allow-public-bind-i-understand A host that sets the flag, or a VPN that admits strangers, exposes the daemon to anyone who can reach it Stolen phone or device token Token hashed at rest, kept in the phone keystore, revocable with porthole devices revoke, connections closed within a second Until revocation the holder has every right a paired phone has; no second factor Malicious prompt in a transcript driving the agent Phone input is literal keystrokes; permission prompts reach the phone with tool name and input for a human decision A prompt approved from the phone runs with the user's rights, as it would in the terminal Relay compromise Notices are encrypted end to end with a key the relay never holds; grants bind one device id and push token The relay operator learns push tokens, device ids, timing and the per-session collapse digest, and can suppress or delay pushes Hook tampering Hook payloads are accepted only for transcripts under a watched profile; answers match a pending prompt id; a hook timeout yields no decision Any process of the same user can connect to the socket and inject events, which equals that user's shell access Local user on the machine State directory 0700, devices.json, tls.key and the socket 0600; the daemon refuses to run as root The same user, or root, reads tokens, the push key and every transcript

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with porthole doctor and porthole status on the machine. Daemon logs: journalctl --user -u porthole -f on Linux, /tmp/porthole.log for the launchd agent on macOS, or run porthole serve --log-level debug in a terminal.

docs.title: Pairing and connecting
docs.text: porthole pair says "no VPN or private address is bound" The daemon found nothing but loopback to listen on. Bring the VPN up (or join the Wi-Fi) and restart the daemon; listen = ["auto"] picks up private and VPN addresses at start. The app cannot reach the machine The phone needs a private route to the host shown by porthole pair: the same network, or the VPN connected on the phone too. The daemon refuses connections from public addresses. Run porthole status on the machine: it lists the bound addresses with their kind (lan or vpn) and the recent connection attempts. If the phone's attempts do not show up there, the traffic is not reaching the daemon: wrong address, wrong network, or a firewall. porthole doctor reports an active host firewall and prints the command that opens TCP port 7433 (or your port). VPN traffic often bypasses the host firewall; LAN traffic does not. The VPN address times out while the LAN address works The phone's VPN client must be a peer of the same network as the machine, with a policy that lets it reach this peer. porthole status shows whether any attempt arrived from the VPN range; if none did, the phone has no route to that address. With NetBird, the phone must appear in netbird status --detail on the machine, under the same controller. The app keeps working over the LAN address and shows the VPN address as unreachable under Machines. "Certificate fingerprint mismatch" The daemon's certificate changed because its state directory (~/.local/state/porthole/) was deleted or the daemon moved to a new machine. Forget the machine in the app and pair again. The pairing code is rejected Codes are single use and expire after two minutes. Five wrong attempts in a minute lock that source address out for a minute. Run porthole pair again. A phone was lost porthole devices then porthole devices revoke <id>. Its connections close within a second and its token stops working.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text: A session is read-only Only sessions running inside tmux can be controlled. Start them with porthole wrap claude (or codex), or from the app's New session. A finished session can be restarted under tmux with Resume in tmux…. See Sessions. A session is missing The daemon reads ~/.claude/projects and ~/.codex/sessions. A CLI using another CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or CODEX_HOME is found while it runs; add the directory to profiles in config.toml to watch it always. Check porthole sessions. No repositories in New session Nothing has been recorded and no session has run anywhere yet. Run porthole add inside a repository, or porthole add --workspace ~/code for a folder of them, then check porthole repos. Permission prompts do not appear on the phone Hooks apply only to sessions started after porthole install-hooks ran; restart the session. porthole doctor reports whether each profile has the hooks. Prompts also fall back to the terminal after permission_timeout_s (60 s) with no answer, so an old prompt may already have been answered at the keyboard. Run with ! says the session is busy, has unsent text, or has messages queued ! only enters Claude Code's shell mode when the session is waiting at its prompt with an empty input box and nothing queued. Wait for the turn and the queued messages to go through, or open the terminal view and clear anything typed there, then try again. If the session is busy for a while, Run in a window runs the command anyway and sends the output into the session when it exits. A message I sent from the phone is not in the chat If Claude was busy, the CLI queued it; the chat shows it as a faded "Queued" bubble until the turn ends. If the bubble says "Could not send", the daemon could not type into the pane; the reason is on the bubble and Retry sends it again. A message that shows neither way was typed into a terminal the app is not following; check the terminal view. A run card stays on "running", or the terminal shows a dead window The daemon that started the run has restarted, usually because the command itself reinstalled it. The new daemon picks the run up from disk, finishes the card and sends the output if asked; the card then says "recovered". A window whose command has ended stays in tmux for ten minutes and is closed by the daemon; the app never follows a dead window, so use Full output on the card instead. Session status stays "unknown" The status comes from hooks, so sessions started before the hooks were installed report nothing until restarted. No account or quota information claude-swap must be on the daemon's PATH. The systemd unit and launchd agent set a fixed PATH; edit it if cswap lives elsewhere, and [cswap] enabled must not be false.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Nothing arrives while the app is closed Direct notifications need the app open (or, on Android, Stay connected in the background). Everything else needs a push relay: a relay URL in Settings → Push relay, [push] relay_url set on every machine, and the daemon restarted afterwards. See Push notifications. "Relay: not active" The relay answered 402: the credential in your relay URL is not active (lapsed, unknown, or mistyped). Check it with whoever runs the relay; for the hosted relay that is https://zerkersec.io/supporter. "Relay: could not verify" The relay could not be reached. The app keeps using its last grant and retries; Re-check forces a retry now. "Apple has not issued this phone a push token yet" The app asks Apple for a push token the first time you save a relay URL, and Apple can take a few seconds. Make sure the phone is online, then save the URL again. TestFlight build 1 never asked Apple for a token and fails here every time; update the app. Relay is connected but one machine never pushes That daemon has no relay_url, or the machine is muted under Machines. The daemon refuses push registrations until the URL is set and it is restarted. There is no Push relay field in Settings This build was made without the Firebase options, so it cannot receive push at all. Install a store build, or build with --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json. iOS alerts arrive late or not at all without a relay iOS suspends the connection shortly after the app leaves the foreground. See iOS background behavior.

docs.title: The daemon
docs.text: "refusing to run as root" Run the daemon as the user who owns the sessions. The service files do this already; do not wrap them in sudo. "listen ... is a public address; refusing" An explicit listen entry is a public IP. Use a private or VPN address instead. --allow-public-bind-i-understand overrides the check; see Security. The service does not come back after a reboot (Linux) User services only run while you are logged in unless linger is enabled: sudo loginctl enable-linger "$USER". porthole install tries this and prints the command if it could not. claude or codex not found by the daemon but fine in a shell The service runs with a fixed PATH (~/.local/bin, /usr/local/bin, /usr/bin, /bin, plus /opt/homebrew/bin on macOS). Add the directory your CLI lives in to the unit's Environment=PATH=… line (Linux) or the plist's PATH (macOS), or point binary in config.toml at the full path. Changes to config.toml do nothing Only repos.toml and workspaces reload live (on SIGHUP or when porthole add runs). Everything else needs systemctl --user restart porthole. See Reloading.

docs.title: When you need this
docs.text:
A push token belongs to the Firebase project the app was built with, and the relay can only send to tokens of the project its service account comes from (relay/src/index.ts posts to https://fcm.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<project>/messages:send, where <project> is FCM_PROJECT_ID or the service account's project_id). So the app build and the relay must use the same Firebase project. The store builds carry the project's own Firebase options, which means they only work with the hosted relay. To use your own relay, build the app with your own Firebase project as described here.

If you do not want push at all, build without --dart-define-from-file: the app then has no Push relay field in Settings and everything else works (see Builds without push).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Platform Needs Both Flutter with Dart 3.11.4 or later (environment.sdk in app/pubspec.yaml), a clone of the repository Android Java 17 (compileOptions in app/android/app/build.gradle.kts), an Android SDK; the app targets API 26 and up (minSdk) iOS A Mac with Xcode and CocoaPods (app/ios/Podfile, iOS 15 and up), and an Apple Developer Program membership: the App ID's Push Notifications capability and the APNs key are registered under it

docs.title: Pick your own app id and name
docs.text:
io.zerkersec.porthole is the project's own id. Firebase registers apps by id, so choose your own (for example com.example.myremote) and set it in every place below before you register anything with Apple or Firebase.

File Change app/android/app/build.gradle.kts namespace (line 19) and applicationId (line 35) app/android/app/src/main/kotlin/io/zerkersec/porthole/MainActivity.kt the package line; move the file to the matching directory app/ios/Runner.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj the three PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = io.zerkersec.porthole; lines (the Runner target); the RunnerTests entries follow the same prefix app/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml android:label app/ios/Runner/Info.plist CFBundleDisplayName and CFBundleName

The name and icon are covered by TRADEMARKS.md: a modified build may not be published under the Porthole name or icon, so a fork picks its own. Icons are generated from app/assets/icon/*.svg with dart run flutter_launcher_icons (see app/README.md).

docs.title: Apple (iOS only)
docs.text:
At developer.apple.com, Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles:

  1. Identifiers, +, App IDs, App. Bundle ID explicit, your id from above, tick Push Notifications, Register.
  2. Keys, +, tick Apple Push Notifications service (APNs), Continue, Register, Download. The file is AuthKey_<KEYID>.p8 and can be downloaded only once; keep the Key ID.
  3. Membership details: note the 10-character Team ID. Firebase asks for it with the APNs key.

docs.title: Firebase
docs.text:
At console.firebase.google.com:

  1. Create a project. Google Analytics is not needed.
  2. Project Overview, Add app, Android. Package name: your Android applicationId. Register, then Download google-services.json.
  3. Add app, iOS. Bundle ID: your iOS bundle id. Register, then Download GoogleService-Info.plist.
  4. iOS only: Project settings (gear), Cloud Messaging, Apple app configuration, APNs Authentication Key, Upload the .p8 with its Key ID and your Team ID.
  5. Project settings, Service accounts, Firebase Admin SDK, Generate new private key. This JSON file is the relay's FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT.

The two config files are not read by the build. There is no google-services Gradle plugin in app/android/app/build.gradle.kts and no plist in the Xcode project; app/lib/push.dart builds FirebaseOptions from the values below. Both file names are gitignored, so keep them outside the checkout and copy values out of them.

docs.title: store.json
docs.text:
cd app
cp dart_defines/store.example.json dart_defines/store.json

dart_defines/store.json is gitignored. Fill each key from the config files (app/lib/config.dart reads them with String.fromEnvironment):

Key Used on Source FB_API_KEY Android google-services.json: client[].api_key[].current_key FB_APP_ID Android google-services.json: client[].client_info.mobilesdk_app_id (the 1:…:android:… value) FB_IOS_API_KEY iOS GoogleService-Info.plist: API_KEY FB_IOS_APP_ID iOS GoogleService-Info.plist: GOOGLE_APP_ID (the 1:…:ios:… value) FB_SENDER_ID both google-services.json: project_info.project_number, the same as the plist's GCM_SENDER_ID FB_PROJECT_ID both google-services.json: project_info.project_id, the same as the plist's PROJECT_ID FB_IOS_BUNDLE_ID iOS GoogleService-Info.plist: BUNDLE_ID (your iOS bundle id)

If google-services.json lists several client entries, take the one whose client_info.android_client_info.package_name is your applicationId. The app treats itself as push capable when the API key, app id, sender id and project id for the running platform are all set (pushCapable in app/lib/config.dart); an Android-only build can leave the three FB_IOS_* keys empty, and an iOS-only build can leave FB_API_KEY and FB_APP_ID empty.

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
cd app
flutter pub get
flutter build apk --release --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json
adb install build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk

Without app/android/key.properties the release build is signed with the debug key (buildTypes.release in app/android/app/build.gradle.kts), which is enough to install on your own phone. To sign with your own keystore, create app/android/key.properties (gitignored) with the four keys the build reads:

storeFile=upload.jks
storePassword=…
keyAlias=upload
keyPassword=…

storeFile is resolved relative to app/android/.

docs.title: iOS
docs.text:
Open app/ios/Runner.xcworkspace in Xcode once, select the Runner target, Signing & Capabilities, and choose your team; signing is set to Automatic in the project. app/ios/Runner/Runner.entitlements already carries aps-environment, which needs the Push Notifications capability on the App ID registered above. Then either run straight onto a connected phone:

cd app
flutter pub get
flutter run --release --dart-define-from-file=dart_defines/store.json
